title: llm 0.37.3
text: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
author: swyx .ai
text: This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann , co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence , that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video What a moving camera teaches you Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing. There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file. What’s worth spending training compute on? One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish. Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. FLUX Kontext examples My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right. Show notes BFL explains what a still image, a moving camera and a soundtrack each contribute during training. FLUX 3 launch and research overview Watch and listen to the results of generating video and sound together. FLUX 3 Video demos See how the lab teaches a model to make a req

title: Show HN: Coral – Open-source gateway where agents write their own tools
author: jcs
text: Hi HN, I'm James, one of the co-founders of Coral. Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on. Agents call tools by writing short TypeScript programs that they can save as custom tools to reuse. You can publish custom tools for groups of agents, so your team’s library of tools adapts to your unique systems, data and use cases. Custom tools help agent performance and give more precise units of permission control. Here’s a short demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p0PKOlHLyVI We started on this while building an AI SRE. To investigate an incident, the agent had to connect the dots across an ocean of telemetry data and undocumented relationships across internal and external systems. It took broad permissions, a lot of tokens and it would start from scratch the next time. We built Coral so that the agent remembers the route. Once a task succeeds, the agent writes the steps that worked into a program and saves it as a custom tool. Next time, the agent finds that custom tool in the same search as standard provider tools (e.g. Datadog, Slack), and reuses it. It started with SRE, but we (and our early users) now use Coral for agent work across the org. For our tasks across GitHub, Linear and Slack with Opus 5.5, custom tools help agents work 29% faster, at 31% lower cost (tasks here: https://withcoral.com/docs/examples/custom-tools ). Coral builds on code mode, adding custom tools, policy controls and managed identities. Each program runs in a V8 isolate with no network access or credentials. Coral checks every tool call against workspace policy before attaching credentials and forwarding it to the provider. You can configure each provider to use the caller’s own account, so teammates can share tools without sharing API tokens. (e.g. https://withcoral.com/blog/slackbot-works-better-with-coral ) Coral is written in Rust, and you can run it as a desktop app or as a shared server. The core is Apache 2.0 and has no limits on users, agents or volume. Everything I've described here is in the OSS edition. SAML, SCIM, and org-wide governance features will be available soon under an enterprise licence. We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback. You can download it here https://withcoral.com/download . I'll be in the comments here and on Slack: https://withcoral.com/slack

title: Deterministic Simulation Testing
author: Martin Fowler (martin@martinfowler.com)
text: Distributed systems are hard to test because partial failures overlap with live traffic and the same fault can produce different execution traces on different runs. Unmesh Joshi describes how deterministic simulation testing addresses this by replacing real clocks, networks, and storage with simulated components driven by a single-threaded execution loop. This allows simulating both hard failures and routine slowdowns—such as network and disk latency spikes—and more importantly makes every execution reproducible. This article explains the technique using a quorum key-value store as a running example, with code from Tickloom, a Java implementation of the approach. more…

title: Egzamin na prawo jazdy w rękach bota
text: Jeśli chcesz dziś zapisać się na praktyczny egzamin na prawo jazdy, w wielu ośrodkach musisz się liczyć z czekaniem przez miesiąc lub dłużej. Możesz też uzbroić się w cierpliwość i na bieżąco sprawdzać info-kierowca.pl, serwis zapisów przygotowany przez PWPW. Co jakiś czas pojawiają się w nim pojedyncze, bliższe terminy, zwolnione przez innych kandydatów albo dodane przez ośrodki egzaminacyjne. Jeśli nie chcesz czekać, z łatwością znajdziesz aplikacje, które za 100+ zł zrobią to za ciebie. Jest jednak haczyk. Żeby z nich skorzystać, trzeba się zalogować do państwowego serwisu wewnątrz narzędzia pośrednika. A to już rodzi poważne ryzyko dla bezpieczeństwa twoich danych. Nowy portal miał zablokować boty Serwis info-kierowca.pl zastępuje dawną platformę info-car.pl i rozszerza jej funkcje. Cyfrowa weryfikacja tożsamości miała, według zapowiedzi PWPW, zabezpieczyć rezerwacje egzaminów na prawo jazdy. Obowiązek zalogowania się i potwierdzenia tożsamości przed wyborem terminu miał utrudnić botom i pośrednikom masowe blokowanie miejsc. W pierwszym tygodniu maja 2026 r. (4–10 maja) w portalu zalogowało się ponad 55,7 tys. osób, a blisko 13,8 tys. potwierdziło rezerwację egzaminu. Zjawisko blokowania terminów istniało już wcześniej. Jeszcze w czasach Info-Car media donosiły o botach wychwytujących i rezerwujących bliskie terminy, zanim zobaczył je kandydat odświeżający stronę. Kandydaci skarżyli się wówczas, że terminów brakuje w systemie państwowym, mimo że są dostępne w płatnych aplikacjach prywatnych. Popyt na takie narzędzia bierze się z długich kolejek w ośrodkach. W interpelacji poselskiej ze stycznia 2026 r. przytoczono dane z info-car.pl z 16 grudnia 2025 r.: w WORD w Częstochowie pierwszy wolny termin egzaminu praktycznego kat. B wypadał za ponad pięć tygodni, w Łodzi i Tychach – za ponad sześć, a w Zielonej Górze – za ponad dwa miesiące. Autor interpelacji zaznaczał, że to stan sprzed wejścia w życie przepisów pozwalających 17-latkom zdobywać prawo jazdy kat. B. Sytuacja różni się jednak między ośrodkami – w części z nich na egzamin praktyczny można zapisać się w zasadzie z dnia na dzień, w innych czeka się tygodniami. Jak działają aplikacje przechwytujące terminy Jak opisuje to PWPW, aplikacje tego typu mają wbudowaną przeglądarkę internetową obsługującą logowanie metodami zintegrowanymi z węzłem krajowym. Użytkownik przekazuje więc swoje dane "niezidentyfikowanemu podmiotowi", następnie narzędzie loguje go do info-kierowca.pl tak samo jak standardowa przeglądarka i realizuje dalsze czynności w jego imieniu. Spółka zwraca uwagę, że chodzi tu o środek identyfikacji elektronicznej, czyli metodę potwierdzania tożsamości o "podobnej randze co np. dowód osobisty". PWPW ma wątpliwości, czy takie działanie jest legalne, i przekazała nam, że zgłosiła sprawę do prokuratury. Tu pojawia się sprzeczność z wcześniejszymi relacjami. Gdy działał Info-Car, twórcy komercyjnych aplikacji zapewniali, że użytkownicy nie muszą przekazywać im danych do logowania. Po przejściu na system wymagający potwierdzenia tożsamości, jeśli opis PWPW jest trafny, logowanie do portalu odbywa się już wewnątrz aplikacji podmiotu trzeciego. Nie wiemy, czy chodzi o tę samą aplikację co wcześniej ani czy zmienił się sposób jej działania. Sesja w państwowym systemie pod kontrolą cudzego kodu Poniższy opis jest naszą interpretacją, a nie stanowiskiem PWPW. Dotyczy każdej aplikacji, która loguje użytkownika do serwisu we własnej, wbudowanej przeglądarce (WebView). Okno takiej przeglądarki kontroluje twórca aplikacji, a sam mechanizm WebView pozwala technicznie odczytywać zawartość wyświetlanych stron i ciasteczka sesyjne oraz wstrzykiwać własny JavaScript. Biorąc pod uwagę możliwości samego mechanizmu WebView, z zewnątrz nie da się sprawdzić, z których elementów korzysta konkretna aplikacja i jakie dane przechowuje. Pewne jest natomiast, że po zalogowaniu w takim oknie aplikacja przejmuje sesję w portalu państwowym, która istnieje w środowisku, nad którym użytkownik n

title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
author: Richard MacManus
text: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It includes companies like Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), don't have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money. Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20. Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s a public company with significant revenue traction . In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare announced record earnings . “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO Matthew Prince . “We crossed $3 billion in annualized revenue with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.” So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, building models is part of a natural progression for the company : from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to serving open weight models like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models. Jev as the “east wind” Chen readily admits that Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models. “And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? We don't have to send every request to an LLM. We can send some of it to a System One model.” In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build Clef — which is a copy of Jev — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model. “All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and inventing something new here , that people cou

title: [AINews] Perplexity hits a $1B revenue run rate, up 4x in 2026
author: swyx .ai
text: Perplexity crossed a $1B annual revenue run rate today , CEO Aravind Srinivas told Semafor at a live event. The Information reported previously under $250M at the start of the year and over $750M by August, with Computer driving some of the growth. At usual agent lab multiples (eg Cognition also crossed $1B , with Cursor crossing $4.6B ), this would roughly mean that Perplexity is now worth $30-50B — if the unit economics hold up. This is a nice bump on the $20B round in September 2025 , and qualifies for our “>$10B fundraise” rule for title stories. Gathering up some recent Perplexity launches for those catching up: Computer. September’s Automations let it pick up recurring tasks where it left off. November’s Teammates take on ongoing jobs. Computer also runs fully locally on supported Macs. Monitor API. Watch a topic or page and get a webhook when something relevant changes. Frontier Research. The new research lab has access to 10,000+ GPUs and plans to publish papers, data, models, and code. Sponsored by Deepgram Deepgram is the voice AI infrastructure behind natural conversation—bringing speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice-focused LLMs, and agents to teams building with voice AI. For any stack and any tools you already love building with, Deepgram slots in as your foundational voice AI technology. So you have control. And we have the context to listen, understand, and speak like a human. Learn more about the Real-time Context Standard . AI Twitter Recap Qwen4-Max in the wild Friday’s Qwen4-Max preview is now a shipping model. At the highest reasoning setting, Qwen4-Max scored 43 on the Intelligence Index, up from 34. Average cost fell from $10.02 to $3.27 per task. Alibaba cut output pricing from $6 to $4.50 per million tokens, and the model generated about 39% fewer of them. Kimi K3.1 Pro cost $3.68 per index task and scored 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to Qwen’s 48%. Artificial Analysis Inside the model. Alibaba kept the total parameter count at 2.4T and reduced the number active per token by 25% to 71B. The model takes images and text, with a 1M-token context window. Smaller open-weight Qwen4 models are still to come. Alibaba Arena and Vals : Arena ranks it #14 overall on Agent Arena, the top Chinese model, with +7.5% net over 14.7k sessions ( Arena ). WebDev : It placed #6 in Code Arena WebDev at 1750, +74 over its predecessor ( WebDev ). It also placed #6 in Image-to-WebDev, just above Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol ( I2WebDev ). Vals Index : It is #11 overall, with large gains in coding and finance ( Vals ). Legal-benchmark caveat : On HLAB it gets 95.7% of checklist items right but passes only 21.3% of tasks, and its output tokens rise 3.6x ( HLAB ). Vision results (independent) : Roboflow calls it underwhelming on its VLM benchmark, with Google, OpenAI and Anthropic now far ahead. At high reasoning effort, however, it is ~4.5x faster and ~68% cheaper per image than Qwen3.8-Max ( Roboflow ). Safety, alignment and eval integrity OpenAI embedded assessments : OpenAI is giving Apollo, METR, Transluce and Goodfire internal access to its models and systems ( OpenAI ). Scope by group : Apollo places six evaluators onsite for four months ( Rundown ). METR reviews OpenAI's largest RL run, with access to transcripts, monitor records and checkpoint snapshots ( METR ). Transluce runs a six-week audit of post-training alignment evals, with a fuller follow-up in early 2027 ( Transluce ). Goodfire embeds interpretability researchers to monitor training runs ( Goodfire ). Limits : METR says its scope excludes the misalignment incidents OpenAI has disclosed and is narrower than METR proposed ( scope ). Criticism of the access terms : Critics say the deals fall short of Sam Altman's promise of "employee-like access." Reported gaps : Assessors get no Slack access, OpenAI selects which staff they interview, and they cannot access weights or run training-based elicitation ( Neel Nanda , Alex Mallen ). Former-employee account : Mikita Bales

title: Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force
author: arshpatankar
text: Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic ( https://axonnic.com ). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots. Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly. The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors. When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies. Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford.
